Silt accumulations in Howard Creek resulting from Bad Creek construction would have an adverse impact on aquatic life. Studies have shown that fairly high flows are required to move bedload sedimentary material in Howard Creek (Langdon, et al., 1976). Providing flow augmentation through the stream diversion structure in the Bad Creek dam during high flow periods has been proposed as a method of shortening the period of recovery of Howard Creek after construction. Storm flow augmentation could also aid in flushing sediments that accumulated prior to project construction, thereby enhancing aquatic habitat in Howard Creek. Applicant should investigate the possibility of providing storm flow augmentation as part of its efforts to restore and enhance Howard Creek.
The SCWMRD and Trout Unlimited have expressed concern that construction of the Bad Creek Project would have an adverse impact on the spawning runs of trout that have been observed in 1 wer Howard Creek. At present, the reproductive success of these runs appears to be very low. Whether or not such spawning, even if successful, would significantly add to trout production in Lake Jocassee has not been determined. Nevertheless, these spawning runs are considered a unique and desirable feature (Timmerman, 1976), and provide the opportunity for fishermen to catch large trout in a small stream. The spawning runs would probably still occur even during the construction period, although spawning success could be adversely affected.
Other tributaries to Lake Jocassee may also be suitable for migrating trout. The Horsepasture River and Toxaway River are both reported to have long expanses of water suitable for trout. It is also reported that large trout have been sighted in these rivers during the winter months. Both of these rivers are located in North Carolina.
